name: No appointment letter but payslips available
expected: Confirms payslips and consistent salary deposits establish valid employer-employee relationship.
prompt: I was never issued a formal appointment letter, but I have 6 months of salary slips and bank credits. Can I claim unpaid wages?
raw_response:
Hello! I am LawPilot AI, your expert and ethical Indian legal assistant, here to help you navigate your employment, tenant, or consumer rights.

### | Your Situation
You completed 6 months of work without receiving a formal appointment letter, and you are now trying to claim your unpaid wages. You possess verifiable proof of your employment and earnings through 6 months of salary slips and corresponding bank credits.

### | Your Legal Position
* Under Section 5 of The Payment of Wages Act, 1936, wages must be paid before the expiry of the 7th day after the last day of the wage period (or 10th day if more than 1,000 persons are employed), making any delay illegal.
* Under Section 15 of The Payment of Wages Act, 1936, you have the statutory right to file a claim before the designated Authority for delayed or unpaid wages, and the authority may award compensation up to ten times the delayed amount.
* Even in the absence of a formal appointment letter, your 6 months of salary slips and bank statements serve as strong presumptive evidence of an employer-employee relationship under Indian labor jurisprudence.
* Under the applicable State Shops and Commercial Establishments Act settlement of dues provisions, commercial and private employers are mandated to clear all earned wages upon the completion of service or termination.

### | Practical Next Steps
1. Gather evidence, including all 6 months of salary slips, bank statements showing salary credits, work emails, chat history, and identity cards if available.
2. Send a written demand notice to your employer explicitly detailing the unpaid wage amount and granting a clear 15-day period for settlement.
3. Appropriate forum: If the employer fails to pay within 15 days, approach the Labour Commissioner or file an application before the designated Authority under Section 15 of The Payment of Wages Act, 1936.

### ℹ️ Information I still need from you
What is the total unpaid amount, and in which state did your employment take place?
